conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: Supported.** The available evidence directly supports the claim that layperson hands-only (chest-compression–only) CPR is associated with better survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest than receiving no bystander CPR. A 2010 JAMA study concluded that compression-only CPR by lay rescuers was associated with increased survival compared with both conventional CPR and no bystander CPR, in a setting that publicly promoted compression-only CPR.

This is an *association* from an observational study, so differences in arrest circumstances, bystander response, and emergency-system factors may partly contribute; it does not by itself establish that hands-only CPR causes the entire survival difference. Still, its direction is consistent with American Heart Association information that immediate CPR can double or triple survival chances after cardiac arrest.

The evidence applies most directly to adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and should not be interpreted as showing hands-only CPR is preferable to conventional CPR in every circumstance (for example, arrests caused by drowning or respiratory causes may differ).

Sources:  
- https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668  
- https://cpr.heart.org/en/resources/cpr-facts-and-stats
